source_refs.note: Book p. 49: 4.2 Matrix Operations, the introductory paragraph before 4.2.1. The list of the four operations follows the sub-headings; Teaching notes, Key points and Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: Matrix operations involve various techniques and procedures applied to matrices. These operations are foundational in linear algebra and have applications in numerous fields such as computer graphics, physics, statistics, etc. Here are some key matrix operations:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
With numbers you can always add, subtract and multiply. With matrices you first have to check the orders:
1. Addition and subtraction need matrices of the same order.
2. Scalar multiplication (a number times a matrix) is always possible.
3. The product \(AB\) needs the number of columns of \(A\) to equal the number of rows of \(B\).
So before every operation ask: "Is it defined for these orders?" Each of the next four pages explains one operation and the reason behind its rule.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where are these operations used? In computer graphics a picture on the screen is moved, rotated or enlarged by multiplying the coordinates of its points by a matrix. In statistics a table of data (for example sales of several shops over several months) is a matrix; adding two such tables month by month is matrix addition. These ideas return at the end of this unit in 4.10.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The four basic operations are addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication and multiplication of two matrices.
2. Each operation is defined only when the orders of the matrices fit.
3. Addition and subtraction work entry by entry; multiplication works row by column.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Treating matrices like single numbers and adding or multiplying them without checking their orders first. A \(2 \times 3\) matrix and a \(3 \times 2\) matrix cannot be added, even though both have six entries.
